claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles can remain structurally and chemically stable during prolonged catalytic heating at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K.
Short-range compositional fluctuations inhibit large-scale elemental segregation in these nanoparticles.
Protective interfacial layers formed in situ inhibit elemental segregation and nanoparticle coarsening.
Low-level addition of a heavier element at approximately 1–2 at% promotes short-range ordering.
Short-range compositional ordering acts as a diffusion barrier against large-scale phase separation or core–shell segregation.
Protective surface oxide layers can form under elevated-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Carbon-based interfacial structures can stabilize multi-element nanoparticles at high temperature by strongly anchoring them to the support.
The heavier dopant creates local compositional perturbations that promote self-limiting diffusion pathways.
The heavier dopant promotes stable, coherent interfaces in the nanoparticles.
Self-limiting diffusion pathways and coherent interfaces hinder coarsening and chemical phase separation during prolonged high-temperature operation in reactive atmospheres.
Compared with undoped controls, doped nanoparticles will undergo smaller changes in particle size, composition, and morphology under matched service conditions.
The doped nanoparticles will largely retain their single-phase character after extended exposure to the target temperatures and redox conditions.
Undoped near-equiatomic nanoparticles will show more coarsening, phase separation, or segregation than doped nanoparticles over the same time scale.
The proposed stabilization requires the dopant concentration to remain below the solid-solution solubility limit.
The proposed stabilization requires temperatures and redox potentials below those that dissolve or destroy the protective surface phase.
Element-specific oxidation thermodynamics and nearest-neighbor interactions govern elevated-temperature surface speciation and oxide evolution.
Interfacial chemistry with the support can influence nanoparticle stability and structural evolution.
Highly oxidizing environments may promote compositional or multiphase changes.
Matched doped and undoped samples subjected to the same thermal and gaseous conditions constitute a control capable of separating a dopant effect from environmental effects.
Equivalent coarsening or segregation in doped and undoped samples would falsify the predicted dopant-mediated stabilization.
